The Lake Prespa bleak (Alburnus belvica) is an endemic cyprinid inhabiting the oligotrophic waters of its namesake lake, where seasonal temperature fluctuations strongly influence developmental rates. Laboratory incubation trials conducted at a stable 19 °C [T = 19 °C] revealed that the embryonic period, from fertilisation to chorion rupture, lasts approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days], a duration that aligns with values reported for other small-bodied leuciscins at similar temperatures. Newly emerged prolarvae possess a minuscule yolk-sac and a wet weight at birth of roughly 0.001 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.001 grams], reflecting the limited endogenous reserves packaged within each small, adhesive egg produced during broadcast spawning. This modest initial mass imposes a brief window for the onset of exogenous feeding, as yolk resorption must be completed before the point of no return is reached. The rapid transition from lecithotrophic to exotrophic nutrition is a critical bottleneck in early life history, and the data obtained at this incubation temperature provide a baseline for comparing the species' performance under the broader thermal regime of the lake.

As individuals progress through the preflexion and flexion larval stages, somatic growth proceeds steadily under the productive late-spring conditions of Lake Prespa. Field surveys employing standardised seining and length-frequency analysis have documented a clear asymptotic body size, with the population's ultimate total length reaching approximately 13.6 cm [Li = approximately 13.6 cm]. This value is consistent with the species' position as a mid-sized cyprinid within its endemic assemblage, considerably smaller than the co-occurring Prespa roach but larger than several miniature gobies. Corresponding length-weight regressions derived from a robust sample of adults indicate that the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown specimens averages roughly 22.7 grams [Wwi = roughly 22.7 grams], a figure that underscores the relatively slender, fusiform body plan typical of pelagic planktivores. Such moderate adult dimensions likely reflect the evolutionary pressures of a low-productivity lacustrine environment where both predation risk and resource limitation may constrain maximum attainable size.

Reproductive maturation in Lake Prespa bleak is closely tied to the attainment of a specific body size rather than a strict chronological age. Histological examination of gonadal tissue sampled across the spawning season indicates that the total length at puberty, the point at which 50% of individuals exhibit active spermatogenesis or vitellogenesis, is approximately 6 cm [Lp = approximately 6 cm]. Fish reaching this size threshold are estimated to have a corresponding wet weight at puberty of about 1.77 grams [Wwp = about 1.77 grams], a mass that represents a substantial increase from the natal condition. The onset of reproductive activity at a relatively small body size is a common strategy among short-lived cyprinids inhabiting unpredictable environments, allowing individuals to contribute to the next generation even under suboptimal growing conditions. Measurements of the gonadosomatic index (GSI), assessed during peak spawning activity when water temperatures reach approximately 26 °C [T = 26 °C], yield a mean value of 12% [GSI = 12%].

The species exhibits a compressed life history schedule characteristic of many small-bodied, fast-growing teleosts occupying seasonal Mediterranean lakes. Longevity records derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith annulus interpretation indicate that the maximum lifespan under natural conditions is approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years], with these data collected from a population experiencing an annual thermal regime where mean summer water temperatures hover near 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. This lifespan is notably extended relative to expectations based solely on body size, suggesting that the stable, oligotrophic environment of Lake Prespa, combined with relatively low predation pressure from native piscivores, may permit slower senescence rates than those observed in more productive, predator-rich waters. The oldest individuals in the sample were typically those that had experienced consistent growth during their juvenile phase and had avoided the significant mortality associated with the peak spawning period, when post-spawning exhaustion can elevate natural death rates. Understanding the determinants of this maximum lifespan is crucial for predicting population resilience under ongoing climatic warming.

Comparative analyses of life history traits across the genus Alburnus reveal that the Lake Prespa bleak occupies an intermediate position in terms of both growth rate and reproductive investment. Unlike its congener Alburnus alburnus, which often matures at a larger body size and exhibits a higher fecundity, the Prespa endemic appears to prioritise a strategy of early maturation at a smaller size. The population-level estimates from this work indicate that the exceptionally low natal mass of 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams] imposes a brief critical window for first feeding, while the maximum total length of 13.6 cm [Li = 13.6 cm] situates the species below the median for leuciscins endemic to ancient lakes. The observed maximum lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years] is noteworthy given the modest body size and likely reflects the low metabolic cost of inhabiting a stable, oligotrophic environment with limited piscivore pressure at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. These data serve as a crucial baseline for assessing the impacts of anthropogenic stressors, including eutrophication and water extraction, on the species' life history trajectory. Continued monitoring of these parameters will be essential for the conservation management of this endemic fish within its restricted range.
